question: to the Commission Alexandra Geese (Verts/ALE), Stéphanie Yon-Courtin (Renew), Birgit Sippel (S&D), Kim Van Sparrentak (Verts/ALE), David Cormand (Verts/ALE), Lucia Yar (Renew), Per Clausen (The Left), Reinier Van Lanschot (Verts/ALE), Markéta Gregorová (Verts/ALE), Lynn Boylan (The Left), Rudi Kennes (The Left) Subject:

Since the appointment of a Special Envoy on AI by the Commission, questions have been raised regarding a potential conflict of interest, as Mr Jim Hagemann Snabe is currently serving as Chairman of the Supervisory Board of Siemens. Siemens is benefiting significantly from the rapid expansion of data centres driven by US hyperscalers1. At the same time, many experts argue that Europe faces distinct constraints, including high energy costs and limited land availability, which require a different AI development model based on high-quality data, efficiency and smaller sector-specific models rather than the large-scale infrastructure approach pursued elsewhere. In this context: 1.

How does the Commission assess the risk of conflicts of interest arising from the appointment of the Chairman of Siemens – a company that directly and indirectly (through Siemens Energy) derives substantial benefits from the expansion of hyperscale data-centre infrastructure2 and is strongly tied to US hyperscalers?
Has there been any influence by the US Government or by any European Member State government to appoint Jim Hagemann Snabe?
How does the Commission reconcile Siemens’ push towards non-green energy3 with the EU’s climate goals?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) 1. Special Advisers are subject to the obligations laid down in the Staff Regulations1 and the Commission rules on Special Advisers, including those relating to conflicts of interest. The Commission carried out an assessment prior to the appointment of the Special Envoy for Industrial AI, to ensure that there is no conflict of interest between the duties as Special Adviser and his professional activities outside the Commission. Appropriate safeguards have also been put in place and accepted by the Special Envoy. Documents forming part of the administrative recruitment process, including the declaration of activities and mitigating measures, cannot be shared, as they contain personal data and are protected in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2018/17252. Furthermore, the Special Envoy for Industrial AI will be in charge of preparing a report subject to public scrutiny where his advice will be visible and accessible to all in full transparency. 2. All appointments by the Commission are based on nothing other than merits and the expertise necessary to fulfil the tasks entrusted to the Special Adviser. 3. Support for nuclear energy is not inconsistent with the Commission’s technology-neutral approach to achieving the EU’s climate and energy objectives. EU’s homegrown energy, renewable and nuclear, play a key role to achieve a clean, affordable and resilient EU energy system.
1 Staff Regulations of Officials of the European Communities, II: Conditions of Employment of Other Servants

of the European Communities, laid down by Council Regulation (EEC, Euratom, ECSC) No 259/68, and in particular Articles 5, 123 and 124 thereof (OJ L 56 of 4 March 1968), as amended by Council Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 723/2004 of 22 March 2004 (OJ L 124 of 27 April 2004, p. 1) and as last amended by Council Regulation (EC, Euratom) No 1066/2006 of 27 June 2006 (OJ L 194 of 14 July 2006, p. 1). 2 Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2018 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by the Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 and Decision No 1247/2002/EC (OJ L 295, 21.11.2018).
